resources.string: How the heart muscle gets its own blood supply
A qualitative view of normal coronary circulation. The drawings show selected routes; anatomy, timing, and flow are not to scale.
Two openings at the aortic root
Blood in the aortic root enters the right and left coronary arteries through two openings, called ostia, just above the aortic valve.

The right coronary artery supplies part of the heart. The left main divides into the left anterior descending (LAD) and circumflex arteries. Smaller branches feed capillaries, where oxygen passes into muscle.
Contraction limits flow into the left ventricular wall

In systole, the contracting left ventricular muscle squeezes the small vessels within its wall. This limits flow into the muscle even while the heart ejects blood into the aorta. Flow can continue elsewhere, including in the right ventricular wall.

In diastole, the left ventricular wall relaxes and releases its small vessels. Pressure in the aorta still drives blood through them. Most blood flow to the left ventricular muscle occurs in this phase.
Cardiac veins drain to the right atrium
After passing through capillaries, blood enters venules and then cardiac veins. Most of it drains through the coronary sinus on the back of the heart into the right atrium.
